title: After Hours

jokes.text: Angela asks if anyone wants to see a picture of Philip, then pivots to her cat Philip — but Oscar's dog is apparently doing baby things too
jokes.setup: Angela shows off baby Philip's booties; Oscar excitedly tries to share a picture of his dog doing something comparable
jokes.punchline: The group treats Oscar's dog pride with the same weight as actual parenthood, setting up the absurd rivalry between pet and human parenting
jokes.explanation: Opens the cold open rivalry well; character-specific (Oscar oversharing about his dog) but the joke is more setup than punchline.

jokes.text: Oscar thinks having a dog is just like having a baby. News flash, if you didn't carry it around in your belly for nine months, it isn't your kid. Exactly. Unless you adopted, of course. That is where we disagree.
jokes.setup: Angela is about to score a point against Oscar by invoking biological parenthood
jokes.punchline: Pam punctures Angela's logic by adding 'unless you adopted' — and Angela's 'that is where we disagree' reveals she's anti-adoption, a dark character reveal played as comedy
jokes.explanation: A tight two-beat joke: Pam's inclusive correction is reasonable, and Angela's casual dismissal of adoption as a valid form of parenthood is a genuinely dark character reveal. The brevity ('That is where we disagree') is perfect — Angela doesn't bother defending it. Strong character integration; only Angela would say this without blinking.

jokes.text: Talking head: Angela and Pam simultaneously — 'Angela is such a liar.' / 'It's maddening.'
jokes.setup: Angela claims her Philip (baby) is already crawling at an implausibly early age
jokes.punchline: Cut to Pam and Oscar in separate talking heads saying 'Angela is such a liar' / 'It's maddening' simultaneously — mockumentary confirmation that everyone knows she's lying
jokes.explanation: The simultaneous confessional cut works well as a mockumentary device — both characters have separately arrived at the same exasperated conclusion. 'It's maddening' from Oscar is the funnier of the two lines. Economy is excellent; five words across two characters deliver the joke perfectly.

jokes.text: 'No one said you must have two. Like her genes are so important. The world just needs more Pam-Jim DNA.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is complaining about exhausting puppy schedules and how Pam says it'll get worse with two children
jokes.punchline: Angela pivots from the puppy/baby debate to a snide attack on Pam's presumed genetic self-importance — a non-sequitur cruelty that's pure Angela
jokes.explanation: The line 'Like her genes are so important' is delivered as a throwaway but lands because it reveals Angela's casual contempt for everyone. Strong character integration — this is textbook Angela Martin cattiness. The 'Pam-Jim DNA' phrasing is specific enough to feel written.

jokes.text: Oscar pivots from baby talk to 'There's nothing harder than taking care of a boat' — Angela and Pam: 'Unbelievable! Un-be-lie-va-ble.'
jokes.setup: Three people arguing about whether dogs or babies are harder; the conversation has real heat
jokes.punchline: Oscar defuses by changing the subject entirely to his brother's sailboat — the most absurd possible pivot — and the women unite in shared outrage at being gaslit out of the debate
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'who has it harder' to sailboats is a perfectly calibrated absurdist escape — Oscar realizing he's losing and fleeing to the most irrelevant topic possible. Angela saying 'Un-be-lie-va-ble' syllable by syllable is a nice visual-performance beat. The moment where rivals unite against a common enemy is a classic sitcom structure executed cleanly.

jokes.text: 'It is the end of the day. It is the end of the week. We managed to fill 40 hours somehow.' [Laughs] 'Pretty good.' 'That's great.' 'Well, thank you. This is very helpful feedback.'
jokes.setup: Robert California marks the end of the work week with the gravitas of a man announcing an achievement
jokes.punchline: The 'achievement' is simply existing through 40 hours of work, and when Andy and someone validate it, Robert deadpans 'This is very helpful feedback' — treating a sycophantic laugh as meaningful data
jokes.explanation: Robert's deadpan self-congratulation for completing a normal work week is characteristically Robert California — pompous, meandering, weirdly menacing. 'This is very helpful feedback' is the sharpest line, mocking the yes-men around him while being one himself about the work week.

jokes.text: Dwight insists he wasn't going to ask about the VP position, then immediately monologues about Robert thinking about 'Dwight, VP. Dwight, VP' — before Robert says 'I can't be hypnotized, Dwight. I tried it, I ended up smoking more.'
jokes.setup: Robert preempts Dwight's VP question; Dwight denies he was going to ask — then immediately tries to psychologically prime Robert
jokes.punchline: Robert deflects with 'I can't be hypnotized — I tried it, I ended up smoking more' — a bizarre, deeply personal non-sequitur that reveals more about Robert than it deflects
jokes.explanation: The hypnosis deflection is a great Robert California joke — it's both a non-sequitur and characterologically rich. The detail that hypnosis made him smoke MORE is the kind of specific weirdness that separates Robert from other pompous boss archetypes. Dwight's escalating 'Dwight, VP, Dwight, VP' chant is also strong setup. High character integration: both jokes could only work with these two characters.

jokes.text: Dwight asks Robert to eliminate candidates not in running; Robert rattles off non-jobs — 'Catching butterflies.' 'That's a hobby unless it's for food.' 'Theater.' 'Waste of time.' 'Dragging.' 'That's just a verb.' 'Dragging sticks.' 'Yes, nice, perfect.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants clarity on who's eliminated from VP contention; he starts listing activities
jokes.punchline: The list descends into pure nonsense — 'catching butterflies,' 'dragging,' and finally 'dragging sticks' which Robert enthusiastically endorses — a perfect absurdist escalation
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire exchange escalates perfectly from plausible (theater) to surreal (dragging sticks). Robert's enthusiastic approval of 'dragging sticks' as a time-filler for eliminated employees is genuinely funny absurdism. 'That's just a verb' is the sharpest individual line — Robert refusing to let bad syntax slide mid-nonsense is very him.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'I tried [hypnosis], I ended up smoking more.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to hypnotize Robert into naming him VP; Robert says he can't be hypnotized
jokes.punchline: The reason he can't be hypnotized is that it made him smoke MORE — a completely unexpected and dark personal detail delivered as a throwaway
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words of unexpected personal history that are both funny and character-deepening. The joke subverts the expected 'it didn't work' by going somewhere darker and weirder. Robert California at his best: a line that sounds like it came from a very strange man's very strange life.

jokes.text: 'English peoples' main use today is judging American talent. You're crap. You're wonderful. They're mean, but they're incisive.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just dismissed three VP candidates with 'not good enough'
jokes.punchline: He muses on the English as arbiters of American talent — doing a brief British accent impression — concluding 'they're mean, but they're incisive' with genuine admiration
jokes.explanation: A moderately funny aside — the British judging American talent is a real cultural observation, and Robert doing the accent is performatively weird in his typical way. But it's somewhat disconnected from the scene and doesn't escalate to anything memorable. Functional Robert California material, not exceptional.

jokes.text: Robert: 'I'm not allowed to say it's mandatory, so let's just call it compulsory.' Dwight: 'I'll be there at 6:00.'
jokes.setup: Robert invites everyone to the hotel bar at 7pm, noting he can't call it mandatory
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'compulsory' — a synonym for mandatory — as if that's different; Dwight one-ups by arriving an hour early, showing he will physically outperform the requirement
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: Robert's 'compulsory' substitution is a nice wordplay/irony beat (he thinks he's found a loophole in his own rule), and Dwight's 'I'll be there at 6:00' is the perfect Dwight response — competitive compliance. The pairing makes both lines funnier than either alone.

jokes.text: 'Maybe we'll see the real Talla-nasty we've been hearing so much about.' 'Talla-nasty, very clever.' 'Wait, you think she invented Talla-nasty?'
jokes.setup: Someone says 'Talla-nasty' as if coining a clever nickname for Tallahassee's nightlife
jokes.punchline: Another character congratulates her on 'inventing' it — implying it's an ancient, well-worn nickname — and someone immediately punctures the moment
jokes.explanation: A light meta-joke about someone thinking they invented a nickname that everyone already knows. Works as a quick beat; not particularly original but lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Cathy talking head: 'I thought I was gonna be hanging out with Stanley on this trip, but he's turned out to be kind of a loose cannon.'
jokes.setup: Cathy describes her Florida trip expectations
jokes.punchline: Calling Stanley a 'loose cannon' — immediately followed by Stanley hitting on random women — confirms the understatement while also being an absurd label for a man just... flirting
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the contrast: 'loose cannon' implies danger, and Stanley's 'dangerous' behavior is just aggressively hitting on strangers. The cut to Stanley proves the point. Functional but not remarkable.

jokes.text: Stanley approaches two women: 'My friend and I are new here in Tallahassee. Would you like to get a cocktail? Maybe go out for a little dancing. Beautiful day, no?'
jokes.setup: Stanley, a married middle-aged man, approaches strangers with the confidence of a 1970s lounge lizard
jokes.punchline: The phrasing is hilariously formal and stilted — 'beautiful day, no?' — as if he learned flirting from a phrasebook. The gap between his self-image and reality is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Stanley's romantic self-image is a rich vein of character comedy. 'Beautiful day, no?' is the best line — pure 70s pickup artist energy from a man who has no business using it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Andy: 'And... bring 'em back up because now the late-night work jam begins.' / 'Say what?' / 'We are good to go!' / 'Say what?' / 'We're good to go!' / 'Stop it. Stop it.' / 'Stop.' / Andy: 'Say—' / 'Andy.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to hype the team for late-night work with call-and-response energy
jokes.punchline: The workers refuse to play along; the repeated 'Say what?' / rejection cycle escalates until someone just says his name flatly — the most devastating possible deflation
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed cringe beat. Andy's desperate energy vs. the workers' complete refusal to engage escalates nicely, and the final 'Andy.' as a full stop is the ideal deadpan kill. Very Andy — his obliviousness in the face of rejection is his core character comedy engine.

jokes.text: 'Ball droppings can be beautiful. For example, when it turns an awkward soprano into a rich, full tenor.'
jokes.setup: Andy says 'someone dropped the ball' about the late-night work situation
jokes.punchline: Kevin takes 'ball dropping' literally and pivots to puberty — specifically male voice breaking — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A double entendre played as completely innocent by Kevin — the joke is that he's either deliberately crass or genuinely misreading the idiom. Either way, 'when it turns an awkward soprano into a rich, full tenor' is a funny, specific payoff that sounds almost highbrow. Kevin's obliviousness elevates it.

jokes.text: 'Jason Bourne would kick Bond's ass.' 'Jason Bourne has no support staff. His own government's out to get him.' 'Genghis Khan could take 'em both down 'cause he's not afraid to kill children.'
jokes.setup: Idle bar conversation escalates from Bond vs. Bourne debate to historical conquest
jokes.punchline: Genghis Khan wins the fight because 'he's not afraid to kill children' — stated as a completely serious tactical advantage
jokes.explanation: The escalation from pop culture debate to historical atrocity is perfectly timed. 'He's not afraid to kill children' delivered as a tactical analysis is dark, quotable, and earns a genuine shock laugh. The brevity and matter-of-fact delivery are key. Loses points on character integration since this could be generic bar talk.

jokes.text: 'What? It's true. He would— He would eviscerate babies and hang them from poles outside of the villages.'
jokes.setup: Someone questions the Genghis Khan child-killing claim
jokes.punchline: The speaker defends it with graphic historical specificity — 'eviscerate babies and hang them from poles' — as if this clinches the debate about who would win a fight
jokes.explanation: An escalation of the Genghis Khan bit — the graphic detail ('eviscerate babies, hang them from poles') doubles down on the dark absurdism. Slightly less effective than the initial line because the shock value is already spent; this is justification, not revelation.

jokes.text: Dwight's drinking game: 'Everyone empty your pockets. Whoever has the most seeds is the king, whoever has the least buttons is the hunchback.' 'How many buttons do you have?' '40. Always.'
jokes.setup: Someone proposes a boring drinking game; Dwight offers an alternative
jokes.punchline: Dwight's game involves seeds and buttons — two items only Dwight would definitely have — and he always has exactly 40 buttons, which is stated as obvious fact
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest pure character joke. The game only works for someone who always carries seeds and buttons — and Dwight has exactly 40 buttons 'always,' delivered as a self-evident fact. It's specific, original, perfectly Dwight, and the '40. Always.' punchline is economical and sharp. The game structure (king/hunchback for seeds/buttons) is surreal enough to be genuinely funny rather than just random. Strong candidate for standout moment.

jokes.text: Packer wins at Dwight's button game by counting transferred buttons, kicks Dwight. 'And he lost at his own lame game. Ooh, double meaning. The game was lame, and now he's lame from the kick.' 'Quick wit.' 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Dwight insists his buttons aren't transferable after someone counts them; Packer kicks him anyway
jokes.punchline: A bystander immediately explains the double meaning of 'lame' — and then congratulates themselves on 'quick wit' — a meta-joke about the joke
jokes.explanation: The meta-layer of explaining then congratulating oneself for the 'lame' double meaning is funny precisely because it's so self-satisfied. The setup (Dwight losing his own game through his own rules) is solid, and the physical kick is the expected slapstick. The meta-commentary elevates it above a basic physical gag.

jokes.text: 'I'll have a glass of your oakiest chardonnay, please.' 'And I will have a waffle with your mapliest syrup.' 'Sorry, no waffles.' 'Oh, okay. Just forget it, then. Forget it. Forget it.' 'A waffle?' 'A hotel waffle. I know what I want to eat. Is that crazy?'
jokes.setup: Robert orders wine with affected precision ('oakiest'); Erin matches his style with 'mapliest syrup'
jokes.punchline: When told there are no waffles, Erin completely shuts down — 'just forget it, then' — and her subsequent indignation about wanting a waffle ('Is that crazy?') is pure Erin obliviousness
jokes.explanation: A layered joke: Robert's 'oakiest' is pompous affectation, Erin mimics it with 'mapliest' (which is somehow more endearing than pretentious), and then her complete emotional shutdown over no waffles is perfect Erin energy. 'I know what I want to eat. Is that crazy?' delivered with total sincerity is the standout line. Strong character integration for both Robert and Erin.

jokes.text: Ryan talking head: 'Why would Erin confide in me that she's staying in Florida if she didn't want me to make some sort of last-ditch, nothing-to-lose, Kelly ka-who run at her?'
jokes.setup: Erin tells Ryan she's thinking of staying in Florida
jokes.punchline: Ryan's confessional reveals he's interpreting casual conversation as a green light for romantic pursuit — specifically coining 'Kelly ka-who' as if it's an established term
jokes.explanation: 'Kelly ka-who' is an amusingly specific invented phrase — the idea that Ryan has a mental filing system for pursuit strategies named after Kelly is funny. The confessional format (Ryan revealing his predatory logic as if it's reasonable) is standard mockumentary cringe but well-executed.

jokes.text: Andy's team processing orders: 'Eight cases, bright white inkjet. Paid.' 'I'm dying!' 'Processed.' 'And delivered.'
jokes.setup: The Scranton team is doing late-night order processing — tedious work read aloud robotically
jokes.punchline: Kevin's 'I'm dying!' inserted between procedural callouts, treated as completely normal by the others who continue the script
jokes.explanation: The joke works through contrast — robotic procedural language ('Paid.' 'Processed.' 'Delivered.') interrupted by Kevin's genuine existential scream, which is then absorbed back into the rhythm. The economy is excellent: one line, big laugh. The workers continuing without acknowledging it is the right comedic choice.

jokes.text: 'Sometimes I get so bored I just want to scream, and then sometimes I actually do scream. I just sort of feel out what the situation calls for.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has just screamed 'I'm dying!' during order processing
jokes.punchline: His confessional reveals the scream was a deliberate choice — he assesses situations and sometimes opts for an actual scream — delivered with complete normalcy
jokes.explanation: The callback confessional recontextualizes Kevin's outburst as considered behavior. 'I just sort of feel out what the situation calls for' — the image of Kevin calmly evaluating whether to scream — is the kind of small, specific Kevin detail that makes him funny rather than just loud.

jokes.text: Packer to unknown: 'She's going to give it to me, as I'm giving it to her tonight.' [Clicks tongue, whinnies] 'The cowgirl has chosen her saddle.'
jokes.setup: Two VP candidates discuss their chances with Nellie
jokes.punchline: Packer's 'giving it to her tonight' conflates sex and the VP job, then the cowgirl/saddle metaphor — with sound effects — reveals his complete vulgarity
jokes.explanation: Packer's crude double entendres are consistent with his character but not particularly clever. The cowgirl/saddle metaphor with horse sound effects is broad and lowbrow without the wit to elevate it. Functional Packer-as-creep material.

jokes.text: Dwight's counter: 'Well, saddles... [clicks tongue, whinnies] sometimes fall off, especially if you don't properly cinch the girth.' 'What? That's a joke, right?'
jokes.setup: Packer uses the cowgirl/saddle metaphor smugly; Dwight responds
jokes.punchline: Dwight extends the metaphor with 'cinching the girth' — an actual saddle term — deployed as a sexual threat/warning, and Packer isn't sure if it's a joke
jokes.explanation: Dwight's extension of Packer's metaphor using actual equestrian terminology ('cinch the girth') is a nice touch — it's both a legitimate metaphor continuation and a veiled threat. 'What? That's a joke, right?' from Packer is the right reaction. Slightly elevated by Dwight's sincere commitment.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'If anyone's having sex with [Nellie] for personal gain, it's me, and I'm not joking at all.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is in a VP competition with Packer; both are considering sleeping with Nellie for the job
jokes.punchline: Dwight's confessional is framed as if clarifying a misunderstanding — 'I'm not joking at all' — as if the offensive part is being wrongly attributed to Packer, not the act itself
jokes.explanation: The confessional format sells the joke: Dwight's indignation is about credit, not ethics. 'I'm not joking at all' as a closing line is perfect — he wants it on the record. Strong character integration; Dwight's competitive ambition overriding all social norms is the core of his character.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I went south of the border for this. And then I went south of that border.' [Jamaican accent] 'A Jamaican feast, man!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has organized dinner for the Florida team with theatrical buildup
jokes.punchline: The geography joke (south of the border → south of that border → Jamaica) and then the gratuitous Jamaican accent delivery is cringe-funny because of Dwight's complete confidence
jokes.explanation: The geographic escalation ('south of that border') is a decent wordplay setup, but the Jamaican accent payoff is more uncomfortable than clever. Dwight's complete lack of self-awareness saves it somewhat.

jokes.text: 'If I wanted Jamaican food, I'd just hire a bunch of bodyguards and go there.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has proudly revealed a Jamaican dinner spread
jokes.punchline: Robert's critique is not 'I don't like Jamaican food' but 'I'd just go to Jamaica' — with the detail that going requires hired bodyguards, implying Jamaica is a warzone and he travels with security
jokes.explanation: The line does triple work: dismisses Dwight's effort, reveals Robert's wealth/paranoia (bodyguards), and is casually xenophobic in a way that's clearly a Robert California character flaw rather than the show endorsing it. 'I'd just hire a bunch of bodyguards and go there' is highly quotable and only Robert would say it with that breezy confidence.

jokes.text: Dwight introduces Brandon as Val's 'boyf' — Brandon confronts Darryl about sleeping with Val, Darryl denies it. 'Dude, you didn't tell me you were fucking Val.' 'High five.'
jokes.setup: Dwight innocently introduces Brandon as Val's boyfriend while Darryl is right there
jokes.punchline: Brandon immediately accuses Darryl of sleeping with Val; Darryl's friend's instinct is to high-five before logic kicks in — then Darryl denies it
jokes.explanation: The high-five instinct before processing the situation is the funniest beat here — a reflexive bro response that briefly forgets the implied accusation. Good character beat for both men. The cringe escalation of the dinner scene starts here.

jokes.text: Robert trying to defuse Brandon's jealous confrontation: 'Let's get back to the food. Brandon, tell us about these delicious-looking goops.'
jokes.setup: Brandon and Darryl are in a tense confrontation over Val
jokes.punchline: 'These delicious-looking goops' — Robert's completely inappropriate pivot to food criticism in the middle of a relationship crisis, using 'goops' as a food descriptor
jokes.explanation: 'Goops' is doing enormous work here. Robert California calling Jamaican cuisine 'delicious-looking goops' while trying to change the subject is both hilariously tone-deaf and a brilliant character beat. 'Goops' is an ugly word used with complete culinary sincerity.

jokes.text: Stanley asks the server: 'Blow in my ear.' Server complies. Stanley: 'Like I'm on the beach.' [Blows] 'Oh.' [Imitates seagull calls] 'Seagull. [Cawing] And a wave crashing.' [Both imitate waves] 'Oh, that is lovely. All right. That's gonna do it for me tonight.'
jokes.setup: Dinner at the hotel; Stanley apparently asked a server to blow in his ear
jokes.punchline: Stanley escalates the ear-blowing into a full beach soundscape — seagulls, waves — which the server helpfully provides, before Stanley dismisses everyone for the evening as if he's had a complete experience
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly surreal and delightful Stanley moment. The request itself is absurd, but the escalation into a full collaborative soundscape — and Stanley's serene satisfaction followed by 'that's gonna do it for me tonight' — is genuinely inventive. It's very specific to Stanley's vacation-mode bliss and his complete detachment from social norms when relaxed. Strong candidate for standout moment of the episode.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Is this March Madness? I love March Madness.' Cathy: 'Oh, no, that's not this 'cause that's in March.' Jim: 'Uh, this is just the NBA. Professional. Miami Heat, actually. So—' Cathy: 'LeBron James.' Jim: 'Yes, nice. Good word association.' [Giggles]
jokes.setup: Cathy has entered Jim's hotel room under the pretense of a broken heater; they're making stilted small talk about basketball
jokes.punchline: Cathy's 'LeBron James' as a contribution to the conversation — just a name, nothing more — and Jim's deflating 'good word association' reveals how hard both are working to not address the real situation
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is in the subtext — everyone (audience included) knows what's happening, but Jim and Cathy are performing normalcy. 'Good word association' is a perfect Jim line: polite, slightly condescending, and a signal that he's aware of the awkwardness but refusing to engage. The cringe is earned.

jokes.text: Cathy does something with a piece of food (apparently ties a knot). Jim: 'Impressive.' Cathy: 'Oh, please, anyone can tie a knot. The real skill is in untying it.'
jokes.setup: Cathy demonstrates a skill — implied to be tying a cherry stem with her tongue — and Jim calls it impressive
jokes.punchline: Her response — 'the real skill is in untying it' — is explicitly suggestive, pushing the flirtation into unmistakable territory
jokes.explanation: The cherry-stem-tongue move is a decades-old flirtation cliché, and 'the real skill is in untying it' is a well-worn follow-up line. It works in context because Cathy is clearly deploying it on purpose, but it's not particularly original writing. The discomfort of the situation saves it.

jokes.text: Stanley shows up at Jim's room: 'My mini bar is oddly out of rum.' Sees Cathy. 'Oh, hello.' Jim: 'We're watching a game. The Heat game. Just a game.' Stanley: 'Got it. Good night. Careful, Jim. It gets easier and easier.'
jokes.setup: Stanley interrupts Jim's awkward alone-time with Cathy under the pretense of needing rum
jokes.punchline: Stanley immediately reads the situation, says 'Good night,' and then delivers 'Careful, Jim. It gets easier and easier' — implying he's an experienced cheater offering wisdom
jokes.explanation: 'It gets easier and easier' is the line of the episode's Jim/Cathy subplot. It's dark, specific to Stanley's character (known cheater on his wife), genuinely ominous for Jim, and deeply funny because Stanley delivers it as experienced mentorship. The economy is exceptional — five words carry enormous implication. Jim's desperate 'Stanley. Stanley. Stanley. All right, hey.' as Stanley leaves is perfect reaction comedy. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Erin: 'Whoa. The lights are still on.' Andy: 'Yeah, they keep them on 'cause it's less expensive than turning them on and off.' Erin: 'I like how guys just know stuff all the time.' Andy: 'Girls know a lot of stuff too, okay? And nobody knows more than you. Especially me.'
jokes.setup: Erin and Andy are in the hotel kitchen after hours; Erin notices the lights are on
jokes.punchline: Andy says 'Girls know a lot of stuff too... nobody knows more than you. Especially me.' — the final two words ('Especially me') recontextualize the compliment as self-deprecation, admitting he knows nothing
jokes.explanation: 'Especially me' is the pivot that makes the whole exchange work — Andy starts defending women's knowledge, overcorrects into complimenting Erin specifically, and then accidentally confesses his own ignorance. The rhythm of the delivery matters: 'nobody knows more than you. Especially me.' is a small comedic loop that collapses neatly on itself. Very Andy.

jokes.text: [Whispers] 'Get down. It's the fuzz.' 'Shh! Do you want us to get scolded?' 'Shut your beautiful, beautiful mouth, please.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Erin are sneaking around the hotel kitchen to make waffles
jokes.punchline: 'It's the fuzz' for hotel staff; 'do you want us to get scolded' as the feared consequence; 'shut your beautiful, beautiful mouth' — Andy slipping in a compliment mid-crisis
jokes.explanation: 'Shut your beautiful, beautiful mouth' is the standout line — Andy mid-crisis can't help editorializing his attraction. 'The fuzz' for kitchen staff and 'scolded' as the feared punishment are good comic word choices that reveal the stakes are comically low.

jokes.text: Text analysis: 'The moon is huge tonight.' 'Ooh, gosh, the moon one's damning.' 'Yeah, sorry.' 'That's regular text talk.'
jokes.setup: The group is reading Darryl's texts to Val, looking for evidence of an affair
jokes.punchline: 'The moon is huge tonight' is deemed 'damning' — then immediately someone says 'that's regular text talk,' perfectly splitting the group between romantic interpretation and literal moon observation
jokes.explanation: A sharp observational joke about how innocuous texts become suspicious in context. 'The moon is huge tonight' — a genuinely innocent observation — being called 'damning' by someone primed to find infidelity is a perfect paranoia joke. 'That's regular text talk' as a defense is the right counterpoint.

jokes.text: 'You're such a great friend,' dot dot dot dot dot. 'Five dots, Darryl? Are you kidding me? Three dots means to be continued, four dots is a typo, but five dots means: Whoa, do not make me say what I want to say, baby, but if I did, it would blow your mind.'
jokes.setup: The group is reading Darryl's texts to Val; they find 'you're such a great friend' with five dots
jokes.punchline: Kelly has an entire interpretive framework for ellipsis count — 3 dots = to be continued, 4 = typo, 5 = 'do not make me say what I want to say, baby' — delivered with total authority
jokes.explanation: The clear standout joke of the episode. The ellipsis taxonomy is original, perfectly calibrated escalation, and only Kelly Kapoor — the show's texting/relationship expert — could deliver it with this authority. 'Three dots means to be continued, four dots is a typo' sets up logical grounding before '5 dots means whoa, do not make me say what I want to say, baby, but if I did, it would blow your mind' explodes into Kelly's romantic hyper-reading. The structure (specific rules → escalating specificity → absurdist maximum interpretation) is exactly right. The whole group's 'Oh...' reaction confirms the impact. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted in offices. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — arguably slightly above it in character specificity.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'Brandon, Darryl and me? That's ridiculous, right? Yeah. Totally crazy. Puts me in an insane asylum just thinking about it. I'm stranded on Shutter Island over here.' 'You look like Ed Harris. If they stretched him a little bit.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is trying to laugh off the accusation that he's pursuing Val
jokes.punchline: His escalating denial ('insane asylum,' 'Shutter Island') gets interrupted by a completely off-topic observation that he looks like a stretched Ed Harris
jokes.explanation: 'Shutter Island' as a metaphor for romantic confusion is decent Darryl. 'You look like Ed Harris if they stretched him a little bit' is a funny non-sequitur insult that deflates the drama. The pivot from denial to casual appearance comparison is the right comedic move.

jokes.text: 'You want to see a picture of me trapped under a tree?'
jokes.setup: The group is showing photos and making conversation at the dinner table while the Brandon/Darryl conflict simmers
jokes.punchline: A completely random offer to show a photo of being 'trapped under a tree' — the specificity of the image (not just injured, specifically trapped under a tree) is the joke
jokes.explanation: A short absurdist line that works through specificity — 'trapped under a tree' is oddly specific and funny as a casual non-sequitur photo offer. Economy is excellent. Loses points for not being particularly character-specific.

jokes.text: Val: 'You look like Ed Harris. If they stretched him a little bit.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is in the middle of his romantic/insane rambling
jokes.punchline: Val, apparently, has been assessing Darryl's physical resemblance to Ed Harris — and while the comparison is flattering, the 'stretched a little bit' qualifier undercuts it perfectly
jokes.explanation: 'If they stretched him a little bit' is a wonderfully specific physical qualifier — it gives with one hand (Ed Harris is handsome) and takes back with the other (Darryl is a stretched version). Good economy. The joke is in the 'stretched' detail.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Freak, I need a favor.' Gabe: 'Well, then you have to call me by my name.' Dwight: 'Gabriel Susan Lewis.'
jokes.setup: Dwight needs Gabe to babysit Packer while he handles a bedbug situation
jokes.punchline: Gabe insists on being called by his name — implying dignity — and Dwight complies by saying his full name including 'Susan,' which is either a middle name or an invention, making it simultaneously respectful and emasculating
jokes.explanation: 'Gabriel Susan Lewis' lands because it fulfills the letter of Gabe's demand while using the full name to highlight how ridiculous his demand for dignity is. The middle name 'Susan' does the extra work — it's unexpected and slightly emasculating. Efficient joke.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'If Jim has bedbugs, that means they're everywhere. I can't risk them coming back to Schrute Farms. Our biggest attraction is our 200-year-old mattresses.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains why he's helping Jim with the bedbug situation
jokes.punchline: His protection motive is Schrute Farms — and specifically 200-year-old mattresses, which are presumably ideal bedbug habitats, being marketed as an attraction
jokes.explanation: The joke has layers: Dwight's help is self-interested (protecting his farm), and the specific detail — 200-year-old mattresses as a selling point — implies the mattresses are ancient, unwashed, and deeply gross. The fact that Dwight is proud of this and markets it as an attraction is perfect Dwight worldbuilding.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'We gotta find it before it eggs.' Jim: 'Argh!' Dwight: 'Jeez! Describe it.' Jim: 'Brown, shiny, painful bite.' Dwight: 'Could be a bat weevil. Describe its mood. Did it seem sleepy?'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Jim are investigating a possible bedbug; Dwight is treating it like a CSI investigation
jokes.punchline: Dwight asks Jim to describe the bug's 'mood' — specifically whether it seemed 'sleepy' — as if insect psychology is a diagnostic tool
jokes.explanation: Asking about a bedbug's emotional state ('did it seem sleepy?') is an excellent absurdist Dwight line — it follows Dwight's survivalist logic (understanding prey psychology) while being completely insane. The delivery escalates further with 'stressed, but to be fair, it was a tense situation' — Jim playing along is a great Jim-Dwight dynamic beat.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Stressed, but to be fair, it was a tense situation.' Dwight: 'Fair enough. But after it bit you, did it run away fearful, or did it walk away smug, self-assured?' Jim: 'So smug. Like he thought it was funny, like this. [Pssh]' Dwight: 'That's a bedbug. Everything's a joke.'
jokes.setup: Dwight continues interrogating Jim about the bedbug's psychology
jokes.punchline: Jim describes the bug as 'so smug' with a full facial impression; Dwight immediately identifies it — 'That's a bedbug. Everything's a joke.' — as if smugness is a key diagnostic feature
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'describe its mood' reaches its apex here. Jim playing along — describing the bug as smug, doing the facial impression — combined with Dwight's completely earnest diagnostic conclusion ('That's a bedbug. Everything's a joke.') is a perfect Jim-Dwight collaboration. 'Everything's a joke' as a bedbug character flaw is absurdist gold. This is one of the episode's top moments — both characters are at their best, and the joke builds perfectly on its setup.

jokes.text: Dwight checking Jim's hair: 'You are clean.' / then: 'God, oh. So greasy. You should just shave all this.' / Jim: 'Just check it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is checking Jim's hair for bugs
jokes.punchline: Dwight uses the medical examination as an opportunity to critique Jim's hair — the clinical task sliding into personal grooming advice
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight-Jim dynamic — Dwight weaponizing a moment of genuine cooperation to deliver unsolicited criticism. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'So greasy. You should just shave all this.' Jim: 'Just check it.' Dwight: 'You are clean.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is checking Jim's hair for bedbugs
jokes.punchline: Dwight editorializes about Jim's hair being 'so greasy' and casually recommends shaving it — then delivers the all-clear as if he's a doctor
jokes.explanation: A smaller beat in the bedbug sequence — Dwight's gratuitous hair critique while performing a medical service is classic Dwight condescension. 'You are clean' as a formal verdict is a nice touch. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'One thing a bedbug thrives on is heat and carbon dioxide. I am gonna generate myself into a human trap. When I jump into the bed, you are gonna cover me with the sheet immediately. And then we'll see who's laughing.' [Dastardly laugh] 'Yeah. Cover me!' Jim: 'Is this really necessary?' Hotel employee: 'He knows what he's doing.'
jokes.setup: Dwight devises a plan to catch the bedbug by using himself as bait
jokes.punchline: 'And then we'll see who's laughing' — Dwight is personally invested in defeating a bedbug's smugness — followed by a dastardly villain laugh, and the hotel employee unexpectedly vouching for him
jokes.explanation: 'Then we'll see who's laughing' is a direct callback to the bedbug's smug demeanor — Dwight is in a personal rivalry with an insect. The dastardly laugh is perfect physical comedy, and the hotel employee's 'He knows what he's doing' is a great understated endorsement that deepens the absurdity. Excellent character integration: only Dwight would become a nemesis to a bedbug.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Nope, I wasn't bitten.' Jim: 'Okay, well, maybe it's not warm enough in here.' Dwight: 'Oh, it's plenty warm, and I was farting continuously under the sheet, creating a kind of greenhouse effect.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's bedbug trap appears to have failed; Jim suggests it wasn't warm enough
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals he was 'farting continuously under the sheet' to generate heat and CO2 — delivered as a factual tactical detail, not a joke
jokes.explanation: 'Farting continuously under the sheet, creating a kind of greenhouse effect' is funny for multiple reasons: it's technically not wrong (CO2 generation), Dwight presents it as sophisticated tactical thinking, and the phrase 'creating a kind of greenhouse effect' elevates the crude to pseudo-scientific. High character integration — Dwight would absolutely do this and describe it exactly this way.

jokes.text: Dwight emerges: 'I wasn't bitten.' Jim: 'Maybe it's not warm enough in here.' Dwight: 'Oh, it's plenty warm, and I was farting continuously under the sheet, creating a kind of greenhouse effect.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to suggest the trap failed because conditions weren't right
jokes.punchline: Dwight clarifies that he was 'farting continuously' to maintain temperature — a detail delivered clinically, as if farting into a hotel bed sheet is standard bug-trapping protocol
jokes.explanation: 'Farting continuously under the sheet, creating a kind of greenhouse effect' is a great line — the technical descriptor 'greenhouse effect' applied to trapped farts in a hotel bed is peak Dwight science. The word 'continuously' does extra work, implying sustained effort. Well-earned callback payoff.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Is that really how you want to get this job?' Dwight: 'Such a chorus girl.'
jokes.setup: Jim questions Dwight's plan to sleep with Nellie for the VP position
jokes.punchline: 'Such a chorus girl' — Dwight's dismissal of Jim's moral objection using a theatrical insult that implies Jim is naive and show-offy about ethics
jokes.explanation: 'Such a chorus girl' is an unusual, specific insult that does real comedic work — it implies Jim is performing his morality for an audience. The unexpectedness of this particular insult from Dwight (not 'idiot' or 'weakling' but 'chorus girl') makes it memorable. Economy is exceptional: three words carry a complete characterization.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Dwight, Dwight, Dwight, Dwight...' [pause] 'Is crazy gone?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just left Jim's room after the bedbug debacle and his VP scheming confession
jokes.punchline: Jim murmurs 'Dwight' several times in the way you'd try to calm someone — then silence — then Cathy asks 'Is crazy gone?'
jokes.explanation: 'Is crazy gone?' is a clean, economical reaction line that doubles as a character summary of Dwight. The pause before it (beat of silence) is good comedic timing inferred from the transcript. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Packer stumbles out of somewhere with music playing, vomits. 'They don't make these cords in boot cut anymore.'
jokes.setup: Packer has been on a wild night out; he staggers and vomits
jokes.punchline: His immediate post-vomit comment is about his pants ('they don't make these cords in boot cut anymore') — total self-absorption, no acknowledgment of the vomiting
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Packer's complete non-reaction to his own vomiting — the corduroy pants are the important thing. 'They don't make these cords in boot cut anymore' is the right level of specific-mundane detail. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'Pathetic, huh? A real man swallows his vomit when a lady is present.'
jokes.setup: Packer has just vomited in front of someone
jokes.punchline: 'A real man swallows his vomit when a lady is present' — Packer's code of chivalry involves vomit suppression, delivered as genuine life advice
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly great Packer line. The concept of vomit-swallowing as a gentleman's courtesy is original and specific — it uses the language of chivalry ('a real man,' 'when a lady is present') to describe something deeply unchivalrous. Highly quotable, strong character integration (only Packer would have this code of conduct), and the delivery as earnest life philosophy elevates it. One of the episode's better jokes.

jokes.text: Cathy: 'Wait, this is why I exercise like a fiend. Feel.' [Jim hesitates but feels] Cathy: 'Seriously.' Jim: 'Okay, all right. I'm really sorry, uh, I just have to say it. I'm married. I'm very happily married.'
jokes.setup: Cathy has ordered two ice cream items and is eating with abandon; she pivots to demonstrating her fitness
jokes.punchline: Jim finally has to explicitly state his marriage — 'I'm very happily married' — after apparently touching her arm, which triggers the whole scene's subtext to burst to the surface
jokes.explanation: The cringe comedy of Jim having to formally announce his marriage ('I'm very happily married') like a legal disclaimer is the joke — but it's more of a plot moment than a pure comedy beat. The scene is effectively uncomfortable, which is the point.

jokes.text: Cathy: 'Oh, my God! What are you thinking? I know that you're married. I sat at your wife's desk. How little do you think of me?'
jokes.setup: Jim announces he's married, apparently assuming Cathy doesn't know
jokes.punchline: Cathy's outrage at being thought capable of not knowing Jim is married — 'I sat at your wife's desk' — is ironic given that she's been engineering this exact situation all evening
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony works well: Cathy performs indignation at the suggestion she'd pursue a married man while having been pursuing a married man. 'I sat at your wife's desk' as a credential for moral rectitude is the funniest specific detail. The audience's awareness of her scheme makes the indignation land as comedy.

jokes.text: Cathy: 'Can you without running to the other side of the room all night?' Jim: 'Yes, I can.' Cathy: 'Okay. You can watch, not watch, whatever you want to do. Take another shower. I don't care.' [Pause] Jim: 'Okay.' [Sighs] Cathy: 'I am so cold.'
jokes.setup: Jim has declared his marriage; Cathy has performed indignation; now they're trying to return to 'watching the game'
jokes.punchline: 'Take another shower. I don't care.' — Cathy is needling Jim about his earlier defensive shower. Then the kicker: 'I am so cold.' — either a literal complaint about the room or a veiled request to get closer
jokes.explanation: 'Take another shower' is a nice callback jab, and 'I am so cold' is a good ambiguous final line — but the joke is mostly situational. The cringe has been building for so long that individual beats are carrying less comedic weight. Functional.

jokes.text: Pam (via phone) to Darryl: 'My friend Jim would tell you to play it cool. My husband would tell you to go for it.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is asking Pam for advice about Val; Pam is trying to give relationship advice while also processing her own situation
jokes.punchline: Pam splits 'Jim' and 'my husband' into two advisors with opposite advice — implying the Jim she knew before marriage and the man she married have diverged, and she prefers the bolder one
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent line. Pam's distinction between 'my friend Jim' and 'my husband' is funny because they're the same person but carries real character depth — the Jim who pursued her boldly is different from the Jim now. It also functions as commentary on the Cathy situation (Jim is definitely playing it 'cool' right now). Strong character integration; this nuance is specifically Pam.

jokes.text: Ryan to Erin: 'I'm really impressed by how much you've grown. Since I met you, it's like night and day. You should move down here with me. We could be roommates. We could get a dog. We could go to R-rated movies. And who knows, I mean, you're a guy, I'm a girl — Maybe in six months —' Erin: 'Six months?' Ryan: 'Um, okay, I'm in love with Kelly.'
jokes.setup: Ryan delivers what sounds like a romantic pitch to Erin — roommates, dog, R-rated movies, 'who knows'
jokes.punchline: Erin's single question ('Six months?') — apparently rejecting the timeline rather than the premise — causes Ryan to immediately fold and declare he's in love with Kelly instead
jokes.explanation: The structure is near-perfect: Ryan builds an elaborate romantic case, Erin raises one objection (the six-month timeline), and Ryan's entire pursuit collapses instantly — 'Um, okay, I'm in love with Kelly.' The comedy is that Ryan's commitment to the Kelly ka-who plan evaporates the moment he hits the slightest resistance. Also funny: Erin's 'six months' objection implies she would have been okay with the dog and R-rated movies. Strong character work for both. Standout candidate.

jokes.text: Erin telling Andy he should move to Florida: 'You should move down here with me. We could be roommates. We could get a dog. We could go to R-rated movies. And who knows, I mean, you're a guy, I'm a girl — maybe in six months—' Andy: 'Six months?'
jokes.setup: Erin is enthusiastically inviting Andy to move to Florida with her
jokes.punchline: After listing 'roommates → dog → R-rated movies,' she suggests a possible romance 'in six months' — Andy's shocked 'Six months?' reveals both his hope and Erin's obliviousness to how slowly she moves
jokes.explanation: Erin's earnest slow-walk through relationship milestones — roommates, dog, R-rated movies, THEN maybe romance — is perfectly Erin. Andy's crestfallen 'Six months?' is the right reaction. Good character integration for both.

jokes.text: Nellie to Dwight: 'Put your forehead near mine, and see if you can read my thoughts.' Dwight: 'Okay. Seven, one, one, nine...' Nellie: 'No, no, no. Not numbers, no.' Dwight: 'Try again.' [pause] 'Ugh, I'm still getting numbers. Seven, one, one — Is anyone around here thinking the numbers seven, one, one? 'Cause please stop, okay?'
jokes.setup: Nellie makes a romantic/seductive forehead-touching gesture to signal her interest in Dwight
jokes.punchline: Dwight attempts to actually read her thoughts and gets only numbers ('7119') — then broadcasts the numbers to the room looking for the source, completely missing the romantic signal
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Dwight joke. He takes the romantic gesture completely literally and attempts actual thought transference — and the thoughts he receives are just a number sequence. His frustrated 'I'm still getting numbers. Seven, one, one — Is anyone around here thinking the numbers seven, one, one?' as he broadcasts to the room is absurdist escalation at its best. Only Dwight would genuinely attempt mind-reading and then troubleshoot the interference. High character integration and strong structure.

jokes.text: Nellie: 'Dwight, give me a key card to your room. Meet me in seven minutes for some one-on-one time.' Dwight: '[Gasps] Wait, the numbers!' Nellie: 'Mm-hmm.' Dwight: 'Oh. Mm-hmm. There you go. I will see you in seven—' Nellie: 'Seven minutes.'
jokes.setup: Nellie drops the mind-reading pretense and directly propositions Dwight, giving a seven-minute timeline
jokes.punchline: Dwight realizes the '7' in his thought-reading ('7119') was a clue — 'Wait, the numbers!' — and pieces together the rendezvous like a code, delighted by his own intelligence
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff works beautifully: Dwight's thought-reading gibberish gets retroactively validated when Nellie says 'seven minutes.' His 'Wait, the numbers!' gasp — treating his random number sequence as prophetic — is the perfect Dwight-logic conclusion. The scene makes him simultaneously oblivious and correct. Excellent callback structure.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'Win at all costs. Don't respect women. These are the tenets I was brought up with, and they have served me well. But my ancestors never worked in corporate America. They were farmers. And before that, hunters. And before that, time travelers. And before that, me again. At least, that's how the legend goes. The point is they never had to worry about how they got ahead. They just had to put food on the table and not alter the past.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is rationalizing his plan to sleep with Nellie for the VP job
jokes.punchline: The ancestral lineage escalates from farmers → hunters → time travelers → 'me again' — with a casual 'at least, that's how the legend goes.' And the advice for time travelers is 'don't alter the past.'
jokes.explanation: The best confessional of the episode and arguably the strongest pure joke. The lineage escalation (farmers → hunters → time travelers → 'me again') is perfectly timed absurdism — each step is more insane than the last, but delivered with identical gravity. 'At least, that's how the legend goes' is the ideal deflation: Dwight acknowledging this is mythology while clearly believing it. 'They just had to put food on the table and not alter the past' as parallel wisdom is exceptional. This is the kind of Dwight monologue that defines the character. Rivals the 43 and 37 for episode top spot. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in structure and craft, exceeds it in originality.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Andy, this has been an amazing night. Epic. Cool-down fiesta begins right now. I got decaf coffee.' 'No way.' 'I got Romy And Michele's High School Reunion.' [applause]
jokes.setup: The team has finished all the late-night orders; Andy announces the celebration
jokes.punchline: Andy's celebration offering is 'Romy and Michele's High School Reunion' — a very specific, not-particularly-cool movie choice — greeted with genuine applause, which says something about the group's night
jokes.explanation: The Romy and Michele choice is an Andy-appropriate detail — specific enough to be funny, not so obscure as to lose the audience. The team's enthusiastic reception reveals how boring the night was. Functional closer for the Scranton subplot, not especially memorable.

jokes.text: Erin to Ryan: 'That was so weird. Can we just, like, never talk about it again?' Ryan: 'Sure.' Ryan: 'Hey, just so you know, me and you — I don't think that's ridiculous. Dot, dot, dot... Dot, dot.'
jokes.setup: Erin wants to forget Ryan's romantic pitch; Ryan agrees, then immediately undermines it
jokes.punchline: Ryan uses the five-dot ellipsis system — but uses only two dots — implying a downgraded but still present interest, invoking Kelly's earlier taxonomy
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback to Kelly's dot taxonomy. Ryan says 'dot, dot, dot... dot, dot' — five dots, but with a pause — and the fact that he uses Kelly's own romantic communication system to express lingering interest in someone else is a layered joke. It also closes his arc perfectly: he couldn't fully let go. Strong economy, smart callback structure.

jokes.text: Jim tries to get Cathy to leave; Cathy acts surprised. Dwight bursts in with chemicals from the maid's cart. 'Stand back! Aah! Stop it, oh, my God! That burns! What is that?' 'It's a compound of chemicals I pulled off of the maid's cart.' Jim: 'Dwight, there!' 'Oh, God, stop it! Stop it!' 'Big one! Really big one!' 'I can't breathe!'
jokes.setup: Jim has been unable to get Cathy to leave his room; Dwight arrives as a solution
jokes.punchline: Dwight sprays random cleaning chemicals in Jim's hotel room to hunt a bedbug, inadvertently (or deliberately) forcing Cathy to flee
jokes.explanation: The physical escalation of the bedbug plot resolves the Jim/Cathy plot — Dwight's chaos inadvertently saves Jim from infidelity. 'It's a compound of chemicals I pulled off of the maid's cart' is an excellent line — Dwight's improvised chemical warfare using hotel cleaning supplies. The payoff of the entire bedbug subplot being Jim's accidental savior is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight to Jim after Cathy leaves: 'You can't stay here. This place is a biohazard. If I were you, I'd just bunk with Cathy.' [Scoffs]
jokes.setup: Dwight has just driven Cathy out with chemicals, inadvertently saving Jim
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately and innocently suggests Jim go bunk with Cathy — the woman who was just trying to seduce him — with zero awareness of the irony
jokes.explanation: The best scene-closing joke of the episode. Dwight has just saved Jim from an awkward situation without knowing it, and then immediately undoes the save by suggesting Jim go sleep with the woman. His complete obliviousness to the Cathy situation — and Jim's 'scoffs' reaction — is perfect. The joke rewards viewers who've tracked the whole subplot. Strong character integration (Dwight would absolutely say this), excellent economy (one sentence collapses everything), and the irony is delicious.

jokes.text: 'Second best bananas foster I've ever had.' 'Oh, yeah? What's the first best?' [knock on door, it's Nellie] 'Dwight?' [lights go off]
jokes.setup: Stanley is contentedly eating dessert; Nellie knocks on what she thinks is Dwight's room
jokes.punchline: It's Stanley's room — and Stanley immediately kills the lights and pretends not to be there, a perfectly timed cowardly escape
jokes.explanation: 'Second best bananas foster I've ever had' as an opener is good Stanley — specific, self-satisfied, vacation Stanley. The payoff (he kills the lights when Nellie knocks) is a nice physical comedy beat. Stanley's immediate threat-avoidance is character-consistent.

jokes.text: Jim's exhausted scoff/reaction shot after Dwight suggests bunking with Cathy
jokes.setup: Dwight has just suggested Jim bunk with Cathy as a solution
jokes.punchline: Jim's scoff/exhale communicates the full weight of his evening's absurdity in one sound
jokes.explanation: A well-earned reaction beat — Jim's non-verbal response to Dwight's final absurdity. Works in context as a cap to the sequence. Can't score very high without any verbal content.

jokes.text: Nellie: 'Dwight?' [knocking] 'Hello? Dwight...' 'I can see the lights under your door.' [lights go off] 'Hello?' 'Look, the light went off.' 'Just as I said the light went on.' 'Dwight?' [long pause] 'Oh, Dwight!'
jokes.setup: Nellie goes to what she thinks is Dwight's room for their assignation; someone inside plays dead
jokes.punchline: The observer notes 'the light went off just as I said the light went on' — and Nellie's sustained, increasingly exasperated knocking, culminating in a resigned 'Oh, Dwight!' is the closing joke of the episode
jokes.explanation: The episode-closing visual gag — lights going off as soon as someone mentions the lights — combined with Nellie's full committed knocking sequence, is a satisfying button. 'Oh, Dwight!' as a final line (either assuming it's Dwight or blaming him for the confusion) closes the Nellie arc with appropriate absurdist confusion. The callback to the assignation plan makes it land better on rewatch.

tmdb_overview: A power play unfolds in Tallahassee when Dwight and Todd Packer compete to become Nellie's vice president. Meanwhile, Jim receives an unwelcome visitor, and Andy forces the Scranton staffers to work late.
